title: How do you implement a custom watermark strategy (implement WatermarkStrategy with createTimestampAssigner and createWatermarkGenerator), and what is the impact of setting max-out-of-orderness too high (high latency) vs too low (dropped events)?
shortTitle: How do you implement a custom watermark strategy

s1_definition.profdef: A custom watermark strategy in Flink is an implementation of the `WatermarkStrategy` interface that supplies two things: a `TimestampAssigner` that extracts the event-time timestamp from each record, and a `WatermarkGenerator` that decides when and how far to advance the watermark based on observed timestamps. You implement it when the built-in strategies like bounded-out-of-orderness or monotonous timestamps do not fit your data, for example when you need per-partition idle handling, adaptive lateness, or punctuated watermarks driven by special marker events. Setting the maximum out-of-orderness too high adds latency because every window waits longer before firing, while setting it too low causes legitimate but slightly-delayed events to be treated as late and dropped.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India needs a rule for when to declare a business minute closed. The timestamp assigner is the clerk who reads the true time off each transaction slip. The watermark generator is the policy that says "announce the minute closed once we are confident all slips for it have arrived." If the policy waits a very long time to be absolutely sure no slip is still in transit, the end-of-minute report is always late, which frustrates the fraud team. If the policy declares the minute closed too eagerly, slips that were just a few seconds behind get thrown away as late, understating the totals. A custom strategy lets the bank write its own closing rule, for example "close the minute when a special end-of-batch marker slip arrives."
s1_definition.oneliner: A custom watermark strategy pairs a timestamp extractor with a rule for advancing the watermark, and the out-of-orderness setting is the dial between waiting too long and dropping too much.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A custom watermark strategy in Flink is an implementation of the `WatermarkStrategy` interface that supplies two things: a `TimestampAssigner` that extracts the event-time timestamp from each record, and a `WatermarkGenerator` that decides when and how far to advance the watermark based on observed timestamps. You implement it when the built-in strategies like bounded-out-of-orderness or monotonous timestamps do not fit your data, for example when you need per-partition idle handling, adaptive lateness, or punctuated watermarks driven by special marker events. Setting the maximum out-of-orderness too high adds latency because every window waits longer before firing, while setting it too low causes legitimate but slightly-delayed events to be treated as late and dropped.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India needs a rule for when to declare a business minute closed. The timestamp assigner is the clerk who reads the true time off each transaction slip. The watermark generator is the policy that says "announce the minute closed once we are confident all slips for it have arrived." If the policy waits a very long time to be absolutely sure no slip is still in transit, the end-of-minute report is always late, which frustrates the fraud team. If the policy declares the minute closed too eagerly, slips that were just a few seconds behind get thrown away as late, understating the totals. A custom strategy lets the bank write its own closing rule, for example "close the minute when a special end-of-batch marker slip arrives."

**One line to remember:** A custom watermark strategy pairs a timestamp extractor with a rule for advancing the watermark, and the out-of-orderness setting is the dial between waiting too long and dropping too much.

sections.s2_technical:
You attach a watermark strategy to a stream with `stream.assignTimestampsAndWatermarks(strategy)`. A `WatermarkStrategy` is a factory for two collaborators. The `createTimestampAssigner` method returns a `TimestampAssigner` whose job is to pull the event-time millis out of each record, for example `(event, recordTimestamp) -> event.getPosTimeMillis()`. The `createWatermarkGenerator` method returns a `WatermarkGenerator` that has two callbacks. The `onEvent` callback is invoked for every record and lets the generator track state such as the maximum timestamp seen. The `onPeriodicEmit` callback is invoked on a timer and is where a periodic generator emits a watermark, typically `output.emitWatermark(new Watermark(maxSeen - allowedLatenessMillis))`.

There are two families of watermark generators. A periodic generator emits watermarks on a fixed interval controlled by `env.getConfig().setAutoWatermarkInterval(...)`; the built-in bounded-out-of-orderness strategy is a periodic generator that emits max-seen minus a fixed delay. A punctuated generator emits a watermark in response to specific marker events, implemented by calling `emitWatermark` inside `onEvent` when you see a record that signals a boundary, such as an end-of-file or end-of-batch record. Punctuated watermarks are useful when your source has explicit completeness markers, because you can advance time exactly when the data tells you a batch is done rather than guessing with a time delay.

The out-of-orderness setting is the central tuning knob. If you set it too high, say sixty seconds, then every event-time window waits a full extra minute of event time before its watermark crosses the window end and the window fires, so end-to-end latency grows by that much and memory holds more open windows. If you set it too low, say zero, you are asserting events arrive in perfect order; any event even slightly delayed arrives after the watermark has passed its window and is treated as late, so it is dropped or diverted to a side output, understating results. The senior approach is to measure the actual lateness distribution of your source, pick an out-of-orderness that covers something like the 99th percentile of observed delay, and handle the rare tail with allowed lateness plus a side output rather than inflating the watermark delay for everyone. You should also handle idle sources with `withIdleness(Duration)`, because a partition that stops producing would otherwise hold the global watermark back and freeze all windows.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India ingests settlement transactions in explicit nightly batches, and each batch ends with a special end-of-batch marker record. A plain time-delay watermark would either wait a fixed guess after the last transaction, adding needless latency, or risk closing too early. What the bank really wants is to advance the watermark the instant the end-of-batch marker arrives, because that marker is a guarantee from the source that no more transactions for that batch are coming. This is exactly a punctuated custom watermark generator: it advances time precisely when a marker event is seen.

Problem 2 — The bank must also tune how much ordinary out-of-orderness it tolerates within a batch, because point-of-sale timestamps can be a few seconds apart from arrival order. If it tolerates too much, the settlement report is slow; if it tolerates too little, a few genuinely slightly-late transactions are dropped and the totals are wrong. This is exactly the max-out-of-orderness tradeoff, and the demo shows both a too-low setting dropping an event and a reasonable setting keeping it.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo. We define a `BatchTxn` record that is either a normal transaction with an event time or an end-of-batch marker. A `CustomWatermarkStrategy` plays the role of Flink's `WatermarkStrategy`: it has a timestamp assigner that reads the event time, and a punctuated watermark generator that, on a normal event, tracks the max timestamp minus the configured out-of-orderness, and on a marker event, immediately advances the watermark to the batch boundary. A `WatermarkConsumer` receives events and watermarks and decides whether each event is on time or late. A `CustomWatermarkDemo` main class runs the same stream twice, once with a too-low out-of-orderness that drops a slightly-late transaction and once with a reasonable value that keeps it, and also shows the marker punctuating the watermark.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
flink:
  watermark:
    out-of-orderness-millis: 5000   # tune this dial carefully
    idle-timeout-millis: 30000      # mark a source idle after this
```

```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/flink-custom-watermark-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.flink.wm.CustomWatermarkDemo

# Real Flink custom strategy skeleton:
#   WatermarkStrategy<BatchTxn> s = WatermarkStrategy
#     .forGenerator(ctx -> new PunctuatedBatchGenerator(5000))
#     .withTimestampAssigner((e, ts) -> e.getEventTimeMillis())
#     .withIdleness(Duration.ofSeconds(30));
#   stream.assignTimestampsAndWatermarks(s);
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four records, three transactions with event times 10 seconds, 12 seconds, and 11 seconds (so the 11-second one is slightly out of order), followed by an end-of-batch marker at 12 seconds. The stream is processed twice, once with out-of-orderness zero and once with five seconds.

Step 1, Run A with zero tolerance: The first transaction at 10 seconds arrives. The watermark before it was negative infinity, so it is accepted, and the watermark advances to 10 seconds minus zero equals 10 seconds. The second transaction at 12 seconds arrives, is accepted, and advances the watermark to 12 seconds.

Step 2, Run A continues: The third transaction at 11 seconds arrives. The watermark that existed before it was 12 seconds, and 11 is less than or equal to 12, so this slightly-out-of-order transaction is late and dropped. With zero tolerance we lost a legitimate transaction.

Step 3, Run A marker: The end-of-batch marker at 12 seconds arrives and punctuates the watermark to 12 seconds, which it already was. Run A ends with two accepted and one dropped.

Step 4, Run B with five-second tolerance: The first transaction at 10 seconds is accepted and the watermark becomes 10 minus 5 equals 5 seconds. The second at 12 seconds is accepted and the watermark becomes 12 minus 5 equals 7 seconds.

Step 5, Run B continues: The third transaction at 11 seconds arrives. The watermark before it was 7 seconds, and 11 is greater than 7, so it is on time and accepted. The five-second tolerance correctly absorbed the small reordering.

Step 6, Run B marker: The end-of-batch marker punctuates the watermark to 12 seconds, cleanly closing the batch now that all three transactions have been accepted. Run B ends with three accepted and zero dropped, proving the tuning difference.

Final output:

```

2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] MARKER punctuated watermark -> 12000
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] Result: accepted=2 dropped=1
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] === Run B: out-of-orderness = 5000 (reasonable) ===
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] ACCEPTED SAV2001 ts=10000
```

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Batch stream: txn@10s, txn@12s, txn@11s, MARKER@12s
    │
    ▼
  CustomWatermarkStrategy
    │ assignTimestamp(txn) = eventTimeMillis
    │
    ├─ normal event ──→ maxSeen update; watermark = maxSeen - OOO
    │
    └─ MARKER event ──→ PUNCTUATE: watermark jumps to batch boundary
    ▼
  WatermarkConsumer
    │
    ├─ eventTime > watermarkBefore ──→ ACCEPTED
    │
    └─ eventTime <= watermarkBefore ──→ DROPPED (late)

  Run A (OOO=0):   txn@11s dropped  → accepted=2 dropped=1
  Run B (OOO=5s):  txn@11s accepted → accepted=3 dropped=0
```

```
  [INIT wm=-inf] ──normal event──→ [wm = max(wm, maxSeen-OOO)]

  [wm = batch boundary (punctuated)] ───────┘

  1. consumer.consume(txn@11s)

  3.   → strategy.onEvent(txn@11s) → maxSeen stays 12000
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A custom watermark strategy in Flink is how you take control of event-time progress when the built-in strategies are not enough. You implement the `WatermarkStrategy` interface, which is really a factory for two collaborators. The first is a timestamp assigner, created in `createTimestampAssigner`, whose only job is to pull the event-time timestamp out of each record. The second is a watermark generator, created in `createWatermarkGenerator`, which has an `onEvent` callback invoked for every record and an `onPeriodicEmit` callback invoked on a timer. A periodic generator emits the watermark on an interval, which is how the built-in bounded-out-of-orderness strategy works, emitting the maximum timestamp seen minus a fixed delay. A punctuated generator instead emits a watermark directly inside `onEvent` when it sees a special marker record, which is ideal when your source has explicit completeness markers like an end-of-batch record, because you can advance time exactly when the data guarantees a batch is finished rather than guessing with a delay.

The out-of-orderness setting is the dial that everyone must understand. If you set it too high, every event-time window waits that much longer in event time before firing, so end-to-end latency grows and more windows stay open in memory. If you set it too low, you are effectively asserting the data arrives in order, so any slightly-delayed event arrives after the watermark has already passed its window and is treated as late and dropped, which silently understates your results. The professional approach is not to guess but to measure the real lateness distribution of the source, set the out-of-orderness to cover roughly the ninety-ninth percentile of observed delay, and handle the rare long tail with allowed lateness and a side output rather than inflating the delay for every event. You also protect against idle partitions with a `withIdleness` setting, because a source that stops emitting would otherwise hold the whole job's watermark back and freeze every window.

At the National Bank of India our nightly settlement feed arrived in explicit batches, each ending with an end-of-batch marker, so I wrote a punctuated custom strategy that advanced the watermark the instant the marker arrived, which removed the latency of waiting on a fixed time delay while still guaranteeing completeness. Within each batch I kept a modest bounded-out-of-orderness of a few seconds to absorb the normal small reordering of point-of-sale timestamps, and I measured our actual delay distribution to choose that value rather than guessing. I could demonstrate concretely that with a zero tolerance a slightly-late transaction was dropped and the settlement total came out wrong, while with a sensible tolerance the same transaction was accepted and the total was correct. Being able to explain the assigner-and-generator structure, the periodic-versus-punctuated choice, and the latency-versus-dropped-events tradeoff of the out-of-orderness dial is exactly what an interviewer wants to hear.
